title: Every screwdriver type ranked by how easy it is to strip
summary: A completely unscientific ranking, from 'designed to strip' to 'you will break before it does.'

blocks.title: A field guide to rounded fasteners
blocks.body: Every drive type is a small bet between the screw maker and your patience. Some bets are rigged. Ranked here by how eagerly the head gives up, from most to least strip-prone. Science was not consulted, but every entry was earned.

blocks.heading: The official unofficial ranking
rows: Designed to slip at high torque so 1930s assemblers would not overtighten. It still slips. You are not imagining it.
One bad angle from a gouge
The screwdriver doubles as a pry bar, chisel, and paint can opener, which is why nobody owns an undamaged one.
Looks like Phillips, strips like it too
The little tick marks mean 'I fixed Phillips.' It fixed it about halfway.
Japanese standard, no cam-out. Stripped only by people using Phillips drivers on it, which is everyone.
Small sizes round off if looked at
The 2.5 mm key is a consumable. Ball ends trade grip for convenience and round off faster.
Excellent grip until T10 and below, where the bit itself becomes the failure point.
Canada's gift. Screws stick to the bit one-handed. Stripping requires genuine effort.
You will round the wrench first
Six full flats of contact. The fastener fails by snapping, which at least feels decisive.

blocks.heading: When the head is already going
items: Stop. Every additional turn is machining the hole rounder.
Seat the driver with a tap from a hammer - a stuck driver is a gripping driver.
Press harder than you turn. Axial force is what keeps the flats engaged.
Last resorts, in order: rubber band in the head, screw extractor, cutting a slot, drilling it out. The drill is surrender, but honest surrender.

blocks.quote: Phillips was not designed to be driven. It was designed to be assembled by someone else, quickly, in 1936.
